We count all triples whose sum is divisible by \(7\), then subtract those with no entry divisible by \(5\).

A useful observation: if a set has equally many numbers in each residue class modulo \(7\), then choosing one entry from that set makes the sum equally likely to have any of the seven residues, regardless of the other entries.

**1. Count all triples with sum divisible by \(7\).**

The numbers \(1,\ldots,98\) have \(14\) representatives of each residue modulo \(7\). Thus, among triples other than \((99,99,99)\), exactly one seventh have sum divisible by \(7\). (Partition these triples according to which positions contain \(99\), then apply the observation.)

Since \(99+99+99=297\) is not divisible by \(7\), the count is
\[
T=\frac{99^3-1}{7}=138614.
\]

**2. Count such triples with no entry divisible by \(5\).**

There are \(99-19=80\) allowed numbers. Their residue counts modulo \(7\) are
\[
\begin{array}{c|rrrrrrr}
\text{Residue}&0&1&2&3&4&5&6\\ \hline
\text{Count}&12&12&12&11&11&11&11
\end{array}
\]
Split these into a set of \(77\) numbers with \(11\) of each residue and three exceptional numbers with residues \(0,1,2\).

Of the \(80^3-3^3\) triples having at least one entry from the balanced set, exactly one seventh have sum divisible by \(7\). For triples consisting entirely of exceptional numbers, the residue sum ranges from \(0\) to \(6\); only \((0,0,0)\) qualifies. Hence
\[
N=\frac{80^3-27}{7}+1=73140.
\]

Because \(5\) is prime, \(5\mid abc\) precisely when at least one entry is divisible by \(5\). The requested count is therefore
\[
\boxed{T-N=138614-73140=65474}.
\]
